short: The life story of the Prophet Muhammad, told in order, from birth to death.
long: The root means to travel, so a sirah is the road a person walked. The oldest surviving account is Ibn Ishaq's, preserved in the edition of Ibn Hisham, alongside al-Waqidi and the Tabaqat of Ibn Sa'd. Sirah writers accepted material on a looser standard of proof than the hadith scholars did, so a story being famous in the sirah does not by itself make it authentic.

short: The Companions: anyone who met the Prophet as a believer and died still believing.
long: The singular is sahabi. That definition is Ibn Hajar's, and it is deliberately wide, so a child lifted up to see him once counts alongside Abu Bakr. At the Farewell Pilgrimage the number present is traditionally given as more than a hundred thousand. Sunni scholarship holds them collectively upright in transmission, which is why hadith critics examine the chain from the generation after them onwards.

short: The second generation: Muslims who met Companions but never met the Prophet himself.
long: They are the ones who received Islam warm from the hands that had held it, and they built the first schools of law and Qur'an teaching. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, al-Hasan al-Basri, Ibn Sirin and Urwah ibn az-Zubayr belong here, and the Prophet named Uways al-Qarani the best of them without ever meeting him. The Prophet said the best of people are his generation, then those who follow them, then those who follow them.

short: The third generation: those who met the Followers, the last age the Prophet praised by name.
long: Malik ibn Anas, Sufyan ath-Thawri, al-Awza'i, Shu'bah and Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak stand in this layer. It is the generation in which the schools of law took shape and hadith began to be gathered into books rather than carried in memory alone. Together with the Companions and the Followers they make up the salaf, the three generations of praise.

short: The first three generations of Muslims: the Companions, the Followers, and those after them.
long: The word means those who went ahead, the way a caravan sends people forward. Ahl as-Sunnah treat their shared understanding as the safest reading of the Qur'an and Sunnah, on the reasoning that people closest to the source heard the language as it was meant. The modern movement label Salafi is a separate and contested usage; belonging to the salaf is a matter of century, not of party.

short: The four caliphs after the Prophet: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali.
long: Rashid means guided along a straight road. Their rule ran from the Prophet's death in the eleventh year of the Hijrah to the killing of Ali in the fortieth, close to thirty years. The Prophet told his community to hold to his sunnah and the sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs after him, which is why their practice carries a weight no later ruler's has. The title is Sunni usage; Shia hold that the succession belonged to Ali from the start. Some scholars add the six months of Hasan ibn Ali to complete the thirty years.

short: Succession to the Prophet in governing the community, not in prophethood, which ended with him.
long: The word means to come after someone and stand where they stood. The office ran through the Rashidun, the Umayyads, the Abbasids and finally the Ottoman claim, and was formally abolished in 1924. Worth knowing: when the Qur'an calls Adam a khalifah, and Dawud a khalifah on the earth, it means a steward answerable for what he is given, not the political office that later took the name.

short: The whole body of Muslims, across every land and century, treated as one community.
long: The root is umm, mother, so an ummah is a people gathered around one origin. The Qur'an calls this community a middle nation and says your ummah is one ummah, and it uses the same word for other nations, for a stretch of time, and once for Ibrahim alone, a single man called a whole community. In practice the word carries a duty: what happens to Muslims elsewhere is not other people's news.

short: The Prophet's migration from Makkah to Madinah in 622, the start of the Muslim calendar.
long: The word means to leave something behind and cut ties with it. He left with Abu Bakr, hid three nights in the cave of Thawr while Quraysh searched, and reached Madinah to build a mosque and a community that could finally live its faith openly. Umar later chose this event, not the Prophet's birth or the first revelation, as year one, because it was the moment the community became a community. The Prophet also said the true muhajir is the one who leaves what Allah forbade.

short: The valley city holding the Ka'bah, where the Prophet was born and revelation began.
long: The Qur'an also calls it Bakkah, and Umm al-Qura, the mother of settlements. Ibrahim left Hajar and Isma'il in it when it had no water and no people, and prayed that hearts would incline towards it. It is a haram, a sanctuary in which fighting, hunting and cutting the trees are forbidden. Most schools bar non Muslims from its precinct, the Hanafis being the exception, and the law in force there keeps them out of the city altogether. The Prophet lived there fifty three years before the Hijrah.

short: The oasis city that took the Prophet in, where he governed, died and is buried.
long: It was called Yathrib before he came; Madinat an-Nabi, the city of the Prophet, shortened to al-Madinah, the City. Its two Arab tribes, Aws and Khazraj, had been at war for generations and were reconciled by Islam. He declared it a sanctuary as Ibrahim had declared Makkah one, prayed for its measures to be blessed, and said that its hardship sifts people the way a furnace clears iron of impurity.

short: The stone cube at the centre of Makkah that Muslims face in every prayer.
long: The name comes from a word for a cube. The Qur'an describes Ibrahim and Isma'il raising its foundations, and calls it the first house appointed for mankind. Quraysh rebuilt it during the Prophet's youth and he settled their quarrel over who would set the Black Stone by carrying it on a cloak they all lifted together. Muslims face it, they do not worship it; it is a direction, and Umar said plainly of the Black Stone that it is a stone which neither harms nor benefits.

short: The Sacred Mosque in Makkah, the enclosure built around the Ka'bah.
long: Haram here means set apart and protected, not forbidden in the sense of sinful. It is the oldest of the three mosques a Muslim may set out on a journey to visit, and the Qur'an makes it the direction of prayer for everyone, wherever they are. A prayer offered in it is reported to be worth many times a prayer elsewhere. The open marble floor around the Ka'bah, where tawaf is made, is called the mataf.

short: The Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, which he built himself and where he is buried.
long: The first thing he did on arriving was buy the land and build it, with palm trunk pillars and a roof of fronds, and the poor Companions who had no home slept along its back wall. His own rooms opened onto it, and he was buried in Aishah's room, which later expansions brought inside the walls, under what is now the green dome. He said a prayer in it is better than a thousand prayers elsewhere, except in the Sacred Mosque.

short: The mosque enclosure in Jerusalem, third of the three mosques worth travelling to visit.
long: Aqsa means farthest, because it was the far end of the night journey from Makkah. It was the first qiblah, faced for roughly sixteen months before the direction turned to the Ka'bah. Common confusion worth clearing: al-Masjid al-Aqsa is the whole walled enclosure, including the golden Dome of the Rock and the silver domed prayer hall, not only the building people usually photograph.

short: The space in the Prophet's Mosque between his house and his pulpit, called a garden of Paradise.
long: The Prophet said that what lies between his house and his minbar is a garden from the gardens of Paradise. It is marked today by a green carpet where the rest of the mosque is red. Scholars read the saying two ways: that the ground itself is literally of Paradise, or that worship performed there leads to Paradise. Either way it is a place to pray in, not to touch, and crowding others out of it is not piety.

short: The low semicircular wall beside the Ka'bah, enclosing ground that is part of the original house.
long: When Quraysh rebuilt the Ka'bah they ran short of lawful money and left this stretch outside the walls. The Prophet told Aishah that if her people were not so new to Islam he would rebuild it on Ibrahim's foundation and bring the Hijr back inside. So praying in it counts as praying inside the Ka'bah, and this is also why tawaf must be made outside the wall, not between it and the building.

short: The well beside the Ka'bah that opened for Hajar and her infant son Isma'il.
long: Left in a dry valley with her baby, Hajar ran seven times between two hills looking for help, and water broke open at the child's feet. The name is said to come from her words as she banked the sand to hold it in. The well was lost for centuries and rediscovered by Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet's grandfather. The Prophet said Zamzam water is for whatever it is drunk for, which is why people drink it with an intention rather than out of habit.

short: Two small hills in Makkah, now enclosed in a corridor, walked between during hajj and umrah.
long: The Qur'an names them among the symbols of Allah. Hajar crossed the ground between them seven times searching for water for Isma'il, and pilgrims repeat her crossing in the rite called sa'i. Both hills are now inside the Sacred Mosque, in a long marble gallery called the mas'a, and only the bare rock at each end still shows. It is a mother's desperate search preserved as an act of worship.

short: The stone Ibrahim stood on while building the Ka'bah, now under glass beside it.
long: The Qur'an commands that the station of Ibrahim be taken as a place of prayer, and pilgrims pray two units behind it after tawaf. The marks on the stone are traditionally described as the impressions of his feet. It is a landmark and a reminder, not a relic with power: it is not touched, kissed or wiped for blessing, and the two units are prayed towards the Ka'bah, not towards the stone.

short: The main cemetery of Madinah, where much of the Prophet's family and many Companions are buried.
long: The full name, Baqi al-Gharqad, refers to a thorn tree that once grew there. Uthman, Fatimah, Hasan ibn Ali, Aishah, Abbas and thousands of Companions lie in it. The Prophet used to visit at night and greet its people. Its graves are left level and unmarked, on his instruction that graves be kept low and not built over. The domes that later centuries raised over them were demolished in 1926, a decision Muslims still argue over, so visitors find open ground rather than monuments.

short: The age of ignorance in Arabia before Islam, and any conduct that still belongs to it.
long: The root is jahl, which means recklessness and hot headed ignorance rather than illiteracy. The Arabs of that age had poetry, memory, hospitality and law, so the word is a verdict on their worship and their violence, not on their intelligence. It also names a condition rather than only a period: the Prophet told Abu Dharr, after he insulted a man over his mother, that he was a man with jahiliyyah still in him.

short: The year an army with an elephant marched on the Ka'bah and was destroyed, around 570.
long: Abrahah, ruling Yemen, came to pull the Ka'bah down so pilgrims would come to his own church instead. Surah al-Fil describes birds pelting the army with stones of baked clay until they were left like chewed straw. The Prophet was born in that year or close to it, and Arabs dated events from it for a generation afterwards. Abd al-Muttalib's answer to Abrahah is famous: the House has a Lord who will protect it.

short: The small cave above Makkah where the Prophet was praying when revelation first came.
long: It sits near the top of Jabal an-Nur, the mountain of light, a hard climb even now. He used to withdraw there for nights at a time before prophethood, and it was there that Jibril pressed him and said Read. He came home shaking and asked to be covered, and Khadijah wrapped him and told him Allah would never disgrace him. He is not reported to have returned to the cave afterwards, so climbing it is a matter of history, not a rite.

short: The Makkan valley where the Prophet's clan was penned by a boycott for about three years.
long: Quraysh hung a written pact in the Ka'bah agreeing to no trade and no marriage with Banu Hashim until they surrendered him. Believer and unbeliever of the clan were shut in together, living on what sympathisers smuggled past the guards, and children's crying could be heard outside. It broke when several Quraysh who had never been comfortable with it tore the document up. Khadijah and Abu Talib both died soon after, in what is called the Year of Sorrow.

short: The first migration, when persecuted Muslims fled Makkah to a Christian king in Abyssinia.
long: It happened in two waves, years before the move to Madinah. The Prophet sent them to the Negus, whom he described as a king under whom nobody is wronged. Quraysh sent envoys with gifts to demand them back; Ja'far ibn Abi Talib answered by describing what they had been and what Islam made of them, then recited from Surah Maryam, and the king wept and refused to hand them over. Some stayed until after Khaybar.

short: The night the Prophet was taken to Jerusalem and then raised through the heavens.
long: Isra is the journey by night to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, where he led the prophets in prayer; mi'raj is the ascent from there. The Qur'an opens Surah al-Isra with the journey and Surah an-Najm describes what he saw at the Lote Tree. It was on this night that the five daily prayers were given, reduced from fifty at Musa's urging. Sunni scholars overwhelmingly hold it was in body and not only in vision, and the exact date is not established.

short: Two secret pledges by men of Madinah that opened the way for the Hijrah.
long: They were made at a mountain pass near Mina during the pilgrimage season. In the first, twelve men promised to worship none but Allah and to keep away from theft, adultery, infanticide and slander, and Mus'ab ibn Umayr was sent back with them as teacher. A year later roughly seventy men and two women pledged to protect him as they would protect their own families, knowing exactly what it would cost. Within months the Muslims of Makkah began slipping away to Madinah.

also: Second of two in the cave
short: The cave south of Makkah where the Prophet and Abu Bakr hid three nights during the Hijrah.
long: Quraysh had put a price on his head and search parties came close enough for Abu Bakr to see their feet. The Qur'an records the moment in Surah at-Tawbah, calling him the second of two when they were in the cave, and quoting his words to his companion: do not grieve, Allah is with us. The verse is the strongest single proof Sunnis cite for Abu Bakr's rank. Abu Bakr was in his fifties and climbed the mountain in the dark.

short: The written charter the Prophet drew up on reaching Madinah, binding its tribes into one body.
long: It made the Muhajirun and Ansar and the Jewish tribes of the city into a single political community for defence, fixed responsibility for blood money clan by clan, and stated that the Jews had their religion and the Muslims theirs. Disputes were to be referred to the Prophet. Its text is preserved in the sirah literature rather than in the hadith collections, and historians treat it as among the earliest documents of the Muslim community.

short: A military expedition the Prophet led in person, as opposed to one he sent out under another.
long: An expedition he dispatched without going himself is a sariyyah. Historians count the ghazawat in the twenties and the sariyyah in the dozens, though the lists differ, and in most of them no fighting actually occurred. The genre of books recording them is called maghazi, and it is the oldest layer of sirah writing. The word by itself means a raid; it carries no ruling, and it is not a synonym for jihad.

short: The first major battle, in year two, where about three hundred Muslims defeated a much larger force.
long: It began as an attempt to intercept a caravan and became a pitched fight against roughly a thousand Quraysh. The Qur'an calls the day the Furqan, the day of separation, and describes angels sent to support the believers. Fathers faced sons and brothers faced brothers in it. Those who fought at Badr, the Badriyyun, hold a rank of their own; the Prophet indicated that Allah had looked upon them and forgiven them.

short: The battle at the mountain outside Madinah where an early Muslim advantage collapsed into losses.
long: The Prophet posted archers on a hill and told them not to leave it whatever happened. When Quraysh broke and the Muslims began collecting spoils, most of the archers came down, and Khalid ibn al-Walid's cavalry came round the open flank. Around seventy Companions were killed, including Hamzah, and the Prophet himself was wounded. Surah Al Imran discusses the day at length, without softening it, which is part of why the Qur'an's honesty about its own community is striking.

short: The siege of Madinah in year five, met by digging a trench across the city's open side.
long: A confederacy of Quraysh and allied tribes came to finish the matter, outnumbering the defenders several times over. Salman al-Farisi suggested the Persian tactic of a trench, which the Arabs had not seen, and the Muslims dug it in bitter cold and hunger with stones tied against their stomachs. After weeks of siege a winter wind tore the camp apart and the confederacy went home. Surah al-Ahzab is named for them and describes the fear of that month plainly.

short: The treaty of year six that looked like a defeat and opened the way to the conquest of Makkah.
long: The Prophet set out for umrah and was stopped short of Makkah. The terms felt humiliating: go home this year, ten years of truce, and hand back anyone who comes to you from Quraysh, and Umar objected openly. Under a tree there the Companions pledged not to flee, the pledge the Qur'an calls Ridwan, and Surah al-Fath then called the treaty a clear victory. Peace let people hear the Qur'an without a war between them, and more entered Islam in those two years than in the nineteen before.

short: The fortified oasis north of Madinah taken in year seven, shortly after Hudaybiyah.
long: Its forts had become the base from which the confederacy against Madinah was organised. The Prophet gave the banner to Ali after saying he would give it to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger and is loved by them. After the surrender the land was left with its farmers on a share of the harvest, an arrangement later cited in the law of crop sharing. It was here that Ja'far returned from Abyssinia, and the Prophet said he did not know which gladdened him more.

short: The first clash with Byzantine forces, in year eight, where three appointed commanders fell in turn.
long: The Prophet named Zayd ibn Harithah to lead, then Ja'far ibn Abi Talib if Zayd fell, then Abdullah ibn Rawahah if Ja'far fell. All three were killed. Khalid ibn al-Walid, newly Muslim, took up the banner and extracted the army intact, and the Prophet called him a sword among the swords of Allah. He is reported to have described the deaths to the Companions in Madinah while the battle was still being fought far away. He did not go himself, so by the strict usage it is a sariyyah rather than a ghazwah.

short: The Prophet's return to Makkah in year eight, taken almost without a fight.
long: Quraysh had broken the Hudaybiyah truce, and he came with an army large enough to make resistance pointless. He entered with his head bowed low over his mount, cleared the idols from around the Ka'bah, and told the people who had driven him out and killed his family that they could go, there was no blame on them today. Surah an-Nasr, about people entering the religion in crowds, belongs to this moment. He also declared that there is no hijrah after the conquest.

short: The ambush weeks after the conquest of Makkah, where confidence in numbers nearly cost the battle.
long: Twelve thousand Muslims marched out against Hawazin and Thaqif, and some said openly that they would not be beaten today for smallness of number. Archers hidden in the narrow valley broke the front and most of the army turned; a small group stood with the Prophet until the line re formed. Surah at-Tawbah names Hunayn and says their numbers pleased them but availed them nothing. The captured wealth was distributed in a way that tested the Ansar, and his answer to them made them weep.

short: The last expedition the Prophet led, a long march north in year nine that ended without battle.
long: It was called the army of hardship: high summer, scarce water, ripe harvests left behind, and a distant enemy. Uthman equipped a large part of it from his own wealth. No fighting took place. Its lasting story is the three Companions who simply failed to go and would not lie about why; the community was told to shun them for fifty nights until Surah at-Tawbah announced that Allah had turned to them, a passage that is really about honesty when a lie would have been easy.

short: The only hajj the Prophet performed after it was made obligatory, in year ten.
long: More than a hundred thousand people came, and he told them to take their rites from him, which is why almost every detail of the hajj is traced to those days. He stood at Arafah and delivered the farewell sermon there. The verse saying the religion has been completed was revealed on that afternoon; when a Jewish man later remarked that such a verse would have been a festival for his people, Umar replied that it came on a day that was already two festivals.

short: The sermon given at Arafah during the Farewell Pilgrimage, months before the Prophet died.
long: The reports of it are scattered across several narrations rather than one continuous text, and popular printed versions blend them. What is firmly established: he declared blood, property and honour sacred among Muslims as sacred as that day and that place; he cancelled the interest and blood feuds of jahiliyyah, beginning with his own family's claims; he charged the men to fear Allah regarding women; and he said he was leaving them what they would not go astray by holding to. He asked them three times whether he had delivered the message.

short: The Muslims of Madinah who took in the emigrants from Makkah and shared everything with them.
long: The word means the helpers. They were the two tribes of Aws and Khazraj, long at war until Islam reconciled them. The Prophet paired each emigrant with a host in a formal bond of brotherhood, and the Qur'an says they preferred others over themselves even while in need. He told them that love of the Ansar is a mark of faith and dislike of them a mark of hypocrisy, and he died and was buried among them.

short: The Muslims who left Makkah for Madinah, leaving homes and property behind.
long: The singular is muhajir, one who cuts ties and moves. They arrived with nothing and the Qur'an praises them alongside the Ansar as the first and foremost. Emigration from Makkah specifically ended with the conquest, when the Prophet said there is no hijrah after the opening, but striving and intention remain. He also defined the muhajir in a wider sense: the one who abandons what Allah has forbidden.

short: The Prophet's household, honoured by all Muslims, though the schools draw its boundary differently.
long: The verse of purification in Surah al-Ahzab sits in a passage addressing his wives, and a hadith records him gathering Ali, Fatimah, Hasan and Husayn under a cloak and praying for them. Most Sunni scholars therefore include both the wives and that close family, and many add the wider clan of Banu Hashim who are forbidden to take zakat. Twelver Shia restrict the term to the five of the cloak and the Imams descended from them. Loving them is agreed; the boundary is not.

short: The Prophet's wives, whom the Qur'an names as mothers to every believer.
long: Surah al-Ahzab says his wives are their mothers, and in the same surah forbids anyone to marry them after him. He was married to eleven women across his life, nine of whom survived him; for twenty five years, until he was fifty, he was married to Khadijah alone. Several were widows, and the marriages knitted together tribes that had been enemies. Aishah and Umm Salamah in particular transmitted a large part of what is known about his private practice.

short: Ten Companions named together in one narration as promised Paradise while still alive.
long: They are Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, Ali, Talhah, az-Zubayr, Abd ar-Rahman ibn Awf, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Sa'id ibn Zayd and Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah. The point is not that only ten were promised Paradise; others, including Khadijah, Fatimah, Bilal and the people of Badr, were given similar news in separate reports. These ten are simply the ones listed in a single hadith, which is why they are remembered as a set.

short: The Prophet's first wife and the first person of all to believe in him.
long: She was a merchant of standing in Makkah who hired him for his honesty and then proposed marriage. When he came down from Hira shaking, she covered him and said Allah would never disgrace a man who carries the weak and gives to the destitute. She spent her wealth on the boycott years and died in the Year of Sorrow, before the Hijrah. All his children except Ibrahim were hers, and Jibril once sent her greetings of peace and news of a house in Paradise.

short: The Prophet's wife, daughter of Abu Bakr, and one of the greatest scholars among the Companions.
long: She narrated over two thousand hadith, much of it about his life at home, and senior Companions came to her with questions of law and inheritance. When she was accused of adultery by rumour, the community was left in suspense for about a month before verses in Surah an-Nur cleared her and set the rule that such a charge needs four witnesses. She later took a side in the first civil war and afterwards spoke of it with open regret. She died in Madinah and is buried in al-Baqi.

short: The Prophet's youngest daughter, wife of Ali and mother of Hasan and Husayn.
long: She lived plainly; the famous exchange in which she asked her father for a servant and was taught words of remembrance instead is well known. He said she was a part of him, and that whoever angers her angers him. In his final illness he whispered something that made her weep and then something that made her smile: that he was dying, and that she would be the first of his household to follow him. She died about six months later, in her twenties.

short: The Prophet's closest friend, his companion in the cave, and the first caliph.
long: He is called as-Siddiq, the one who confirms, for believing the night journey without hesitation when others scoffed. He freed Bilal and other tortured slaves with his own money, and the Prophet appointed him to lead the prayer in his final illness. His caliphate lasted about two years and was mostly spent holding the community together through the wars of apostasy; he also ordered the Qur'an gathered into a single written copy. He is buried beside the Prophet.

short: The second caliph, called al-Faruq, under whom the Muslim state expanded enormously.
long: He had set out to kill the Prophet and accepted Islam on the road, after hearing Surah Ta Ha in his sister's house. As caliph for about ten years he took Syria, Egypt, Iraq and Persia, and built the machinery of a state: a treasury, a stipend register, provincial governors held to account, and the Hijri calendar. Several rulings were revealed in line with opinions he had voiced. He walked Madinah at night without guards, and was stabbed while leading fajr.

short: The third caliph, called Dhun-Nurayn, who fixed the Qur'an in one agreed written text.
long: The title means possessor of two lights, because he married two of the Prophet's daughters in turn. He was wealthy and gave heavily: he bought the well of Rumah for the people of Madinah and equipped much of the army of Tabuk. His great act as caliph was to standardise the mushaf, sending official copies to the provinces when he saw reciters disputing over readings. Rebels besieged his house and killed him while he was reading the Qur'an; he refused to let anyone fight for him.

short: The Prophet's cousin and son in law, raised by him, and the fourth caliph.
long: He was the first child to accept Islam and slept in the Prophet's bed on the night of the Hijrah so the assassins would think he was still there. He married Fatimah, carried the banner at Khaybar, and was known for both learning and courage. His caliphate, from the thirty fifth to the fortieth year, was consumed by the first civil war; he moved the capital to Kufa and was killed in its mosque. Sunnis count him the fourth of the rightly guided caliphs; Shia hold him to be the first Imam and the rightful successor from the start.

short: The Prophet's uncle, called the Lion of Allah, killed at Uhud.
long: He accepted Islam in anger, hearing that Abu Jahl had abused his nephew, and his conversion changed the balance of pressure on the Muslims in Makkah. He fought at Badr and was killed at Uhud by Wahshi, a man promised his freedom for the deed, and the Prophet was profoundly grieved by the state of his body. Years later Wahshi accepted Islam and was forgiven, though the Prophet asked him to keep his face out of sight. Hamzah is remembered as the chief of the martyrs.

short: An enslaved Abyssinian tortured for his faith, freed by Abu Bakr, and the first to call the adhan.
long: His owner pinned him under a rock in the midday heat of Makkah and he answered only with one word, ahad, one. Abu Bakr bought him and set him free. When the Muslims settled in Madinah and needed a way to gather people, he was given the call to prayer, and on the day Makkah was taken he climbed onto the Ka'bah to make it. The Prophet told him he had heard his footsteps ahead of him in Paradise, and Bilal explained he prayed after every wudu.

short: The best dressed youth in Makkah who gave it up, taught Madinah Islam, and died at Uhud.
long: His mother had raised him in luxury and cut him off when he believed. After the first pledge at Aqabah the Prophet sent him alone to Madinah as teacher and reciter, and through him whole households of the Aws and Khazraj entered Islam before the Hijrah. He carried the banner at Uhud and was killed there. When they came to bury him they had only one short cloak: covering his head left his feet bare, and covering his feet left his head bare.

short: The commander called the Sword of Allah, who fought against the Muslims before joining them.
long: His cavalry turned the day against the Muslims at Uhud. He accepted Islam before the conquest of Makkah, saved the army at Mu'tah, and then led the campaigns against the false prophets and into Syria, where Yarmuk broke Byzantine power in the region. Umar removed him from command while he was winning, reportedly so people would learn that victory comes from Allah and not from a man. He accepted it and served under his replacement, and died in his bed in Homs.

short: A Persian who searched through two religions for the truth and was enslaved before finding it.
long: He left his father's fire worship for Christianity, served a succession of monks, and was told by the last of them that a prophet was about to appear in a land of date palms. On the way he was betrayed and sold as a slave into Madinah, where he recognised the signs he had been described. The Companions helped him buy his freedom. At the Trench it was his suggestion, unknown to the Arabs, that saved the city, and the Prophet is reported to have said Salman is of us, the people of the house.

short: The Companion who narrated more hadith than any other, from about four years in the Prophet's company.
long: The nickname means father of the kitten, from a cat he carried as a boy. He accepted Islam around the year of Khaybar, joined the poor Companions living on the mosque bench, and stayed close to the Prophet while others worked or traded. He said openly that the Muhajirun were busy in the markets and the Ansar with their land, and he was not. He also asked the Prophet to pray that he would not forget, and reported that he never forgot anything afterwards.

also: Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib
short: The Prophet's elder grandson, who gave up the caliphate to stop a war between Muslims.
long: After Ali was killed the people of Iraq pledged to him, and Mu'awiyah held Syria. Rather than fight, he negotiated terms and stepped aside in the forty first year, and that year is called the Year of Unity. The Prophet had said of him, while he was a child on the pulpit, that this son of his is a master and that Allah would reconcile two great parties of Muslims through him. Twelver Shia count him the second Imam, and he is buried in al-Baqi.

short: The Prophet's younger grandson, killed at Karbala in the sixty first year of the Hijrah.
long: When Mu'awiyah died and rule passed to his son Yazid, Husayn refused to pledge allegiance and set out for Kufa on the invitation of its people. They abandoned him, and he was surrounded at Karbala with a small band of family and followers, cut off from water, and killed with most of the men of his household. The Prophet had said that he and Hasan were the masters of the youth of Paradise. His death remains one of the deepest wounds in Muslim memory.

short: Abu Bakr's campaigns against tribes that broke away after the Prophet died.
long: Some tribes rejected Islam outright, some followed men claiming prophethood such as Musaylimah, and some kept the prayer but refused to pay zakat to Madinah. Abu Bakr insisted on all of it, saying he would fight anyone who separated what the Prophet had joined, and Umar, who had hesitated, came to agree. The heaviest battle was Yamamah, where so many memorisers of the Qur'an were killed that Umar urged Abu Bakr to have it collected in one written copy.

short: The first civil war among Muslims, from the killing of Uthman to the death of Ali.
long: Fitnah means a fire that tests metal, and then any trial that separates people. It ran from the thirty fifth to the fortieth year of the Hijrah: the murder of Uthman, the Battle of the Camel, Siffin, the failed arbitration, and the breaking away of the Kharijites who then killed Ali. Sunni scholarship holds that both sides were Companions acting on interpretation, that Ali was closer to the truth, and that the settled adab is to restrain the tongue about what happened.

short: The plain in Iraq where Husayn and his household were killed on the tenth of Muharram, year 61.
long: He had refused to pledge to Yazid and was travelling to Kufa when the army sent to intercept him cut him off from the Euphrates. Around seventy of his party were killed, including his family, and the survivors were taken to Damascus. Sunnis regard it as a grievous crime and grieve it without ritual observance, while Twelver Shia commemorate it every Muharram as a central act of devotion. Whatever a Muslim's school, the grandson of the Prophet was killed by people who called themselves Muslims.

short: The first dynasty of caliphs, ruling from Damascus for about ninety years after the Rashidun.
long: It began with Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan, a Companion and scribe of revelation, and turned the caliphate into an inherited office. Under them the state reached Spain in the west and the Indus in the east, Arabic became the language of administration, coinage was reformed, and the Dome of the Rock was built. Muslim assessment of them is mixed and always has been. Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, the exception nearly everyone praises, came from this family.

short: The Umayyad caliph whose short reign is remembered as a return to the way of the Rashidun.
long: He ruled about two and a half years from the ninety ninth year of the Hijrah. He returned property his family had taken, stopped the cursing of Ali from the pulpits, lightened taxes on new Muslims, and lived so plainly that his own household noticed the change first. He is also the caliph who ordered hadith to be gathered and written down systematically, which is why so much survives. Many scholars call him the fifth of the rightly guided caliphs.

short: The earliest of the four imams, a Kufan merchant whose school is the most widely followed today.
long: He was born around the year 80 and died in 150, in Baghdad. He is often counted among the Tabi'un on the basis that he may have seen the Companion Anas ibn Malik as a child, though scholars discuss this. He taught by argument in a circle rather than by dictation, and his students Abu Yusuf and Muhammad ash-Shaybani wrote the school down. He refused the post of chief judge and died in prison, and he is remembered as much for that refusal as for his law.

short: The imam of Madinah, who taught in the Prophet's mosque and wrote the Muwatta.
long: He died in 179 and spent almost his whole life in the city, on the reasoning that its inherited practice was itself a form of evidence. The Muwatta is among the earliest surviving books to put hadith and legal rulings side by side. He was flogged for a ruling that displeased the authorities and did not retract it. When a caliph proposed making his book the single law of the empire he refused, saying the Companions had scattered and people had learned different things.

short: The imam who wrote the first book on how law is derived, bridging Madinah and Iraq.
long: Born in Gaza in 150 and died in Egypt in 204, of the Prophet's wider clan. He memorised the Muwatta and studied with Malik in Madinah, then with Abu Hanifah's student ash-Shaybani in Iraq, and so held both approaches in one head. His Risalah set out the sources of law in order and is the foundation of usul al-fiqh as a discipline. He revised his own positions after moving to Egypt, which is why the school records an old and a new opinion on some questions.

short: The imam of hadith who was flogged rather than say the Qur'an was created.
long: He died in 241 in Baghdad. His Musnad gathers tens of thousands of reports arranged by the Companion who narrated them rather than by subject. Under three caliphs he was put to the test over the doctrine that the Qur'an is created, imprisoned and beaten, and refused; when the policy was finally reversed his stand was seen as having held the community's creed steady. He is reported to have forgiven the man who flogged him, and he resisted having his opinions written down as a school at all.

short: The scholar from Bukhara who compiled the Sahih, the most rigorously sifted book of hadith.
long: Born in 194, he lost his sight as a child and had it restored, and began memorising hadith before he was ten. He travelled for years across the Muslim world collecting reports, and required proof that a narrator had actually met the person he quoted, a stricter condition than most. Beyond the Sahih he wrote al-Adab al-Mufrad on manners and at-Tarikh al-Kabir on narrators. He died in exile near Samarqand in 256, after a dispute over a theological question.

short: The compiler of the second Sahih, a student and close friend of al-Bukhari.
long: He was from Nishapur and died in 261, a few years after his teacher. He held that two narrators living in the same period with the possibility of meeting is enough, without proof of an actual meeting, which is the main methodological difference between the two books. He gathered every chain of a hadith in one place instead of scattering them, which makes his book easier to study. His introduction is a short treatise on hadith criticism and is still read on its own.

short: The Muslim lunar calendar, counting years from the Hijrah and running about eleven days shorter than the solar year.
long: Umar established it, choosing the Hijrah as year one rather than the Prophet's birth or the first revelation. Its twelve months are Muharram, Safar, Rabi al-Awwal, Rabi ath-Thani, Jumada al-Ula, Jumada al-Akhirah, Rajab, Sha'ban, Ramadan, Shawwal, Dhul Qa'dah and Dhul Hijjah, and four of them are sacred. Because it is purely lunar, Ramadan and hajj move through all the seasons over roughly thirty three years, so every generation fasts both the long days and the short ones.

short: The tenth of Muharram, a day the Prophet fasted for the deliverance of Musa from Pharaoh.
long: Arriving in Madinah he found the Jews fasting it and said that he had more right to Musa than they did. Fasting it is recommended and is reported to expiate the previous year; he intended to add the ninth as well, so most fast both. It is also the day Husayn was killed at Karbala in the sixty first year. Sunnis do not treat it as a day of mourning ritual, while Twelver Shia observe it as the central commemoration of that loss.
